en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Requiring Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa)
4. The Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Monastery.
Now at that time, some Sakyans who were slaves had been imprisoned.
The Śākyan women wished to provide meals at forest lodgings.
The Śākyan slaves heard:
"It seems the Śākyan women wish to provide meals at forest lodgings."
They fell upon those paths.
The Śākyan women, taking fine hard and soft food, went to a forest dwelling.
The Śākyan slaves, having gone out, seized and violated the Śākyan women.
The Sakyans, having gone out and seized those thieves together with their goods, complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can it be that the venerable ones did not report the presence of thieves dwelling in the monastery?
The monks heard the Sakyans complaining, grumbling, and becoming indignant.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, I shall lay down a training rule for the bhikkhus based on ten reasons: for the welfare of the Saṅgha... [and so forth].”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Now, regarding those forest lodgings that are considered risky and dangerous,
whatever monk, in such lodgings, should [accept] fresh or cooked food without having previously informed [the owners]..."
“If, within a monastery, one should accept with one’s own hand and then eat or consume [food], that bhikkhu must confess:
‘Friends, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable offense entailing confession; I confess it.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was ill in a forest dwelling.
People, taking hard food or soft food, went to that forest dwelling.
Then those people said this to that bhikkhu:
“Eat, venerable sir.
Then that bhikkhu thought:
“The Blessed One has prohibited [us] from taking hard food or soft food with our own hands in forest lodgings.”
Being anxious about whether he could accept it to eat and consume, he did not accept it;
he was unable to go for alms and his meal was cut short.
Then that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, for a sick monk staying in forest lodgings, to receive fresh or cooked food with his own hands even without prior announcement, and to eat it.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus: “Now,
regarding those forest lodgings that are considered risky and dangerous,
if any monk, in such lodgings, should eat fresh or cooked food without having previously informed [the owners], [he commits an offense].”
If, within a monastery, a monk who is not ill should, with his own hand, accept [food] and eat or consume it, that monk must confess:
"Friends, I have committed a blameworthy matter, an unseemly offense entailing confession;
I confess it. As for those forest lodgings...
A forest dwelling (*āraññaka*) is a resting place that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant [from inhabited areas].
A place is considered "dangerous" (*sāsaṅka*) if,

within the monastery grounds (*ārāma*) or its vicinity (*ārāmūpacāra*), the site where thieves have encamped is seen, or their place of eating is seen, or their place of standing is seen, or their place of sitting is seen, or their place of lying down is seen.
"Perilous" means that in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery, people are seen being killed by thieves, seen being plundered, or seen being beaten. "But whoever...
[refers to the following].
Whoever is such a one...
[as described] ...a bhikkhu... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"In such resting places" means in resting places of this kind.
"Without having informed" means:
That which is enclosed within the five [types of dwellings] is what is called "unenclosed.
With the exception of the monastery and its precincts, that which is enclosed is what is called "unenclosed.
This is what is meant by "enclosed."
If any woman or man comes to the monastery or its vicinity and announces, "Venerable sir,
such-and-such a person will bring hard food or soft food," if it is dangerous,
it should be declared as dangerous; if it is perilous, it should be declared as perilous.
If he says, “Let it be, venerable sir, it will be brought,” then the thieves should be told, “People are frequenting this place; move away.
When rice porridge has been announced, its accompaniments are brought; this is what is called “announced.
When a meal has been announced, its accompaniments are brought; this is what is called “announced.”
When it has been announced by means of solid food, his retinue is brought [to the meal]; this is called "announced.
When it has been announced by means of a family, whichever person from that family brings either solid food or soft food; this is called "announced.
When it has been announced by means of a village, whichever person from that village brings either solid food or soft food; this is called "announced."
When it has been announced by a group, whatever solid food or soft food a person from that group brings, this is called "announced.
Solid food means:
with the exception of the five kinds of cooked food, the post-midday tonics, the seven-day tonics, and the lifetime tonics, the remainder is called solid food.
"Edible food" means the five kinds of cooked food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
"Within the monastery grounds" means...
The interior of an enclosed monastery is "within the monastery.
For an unenclosed one, it is the precincts.
One who is not ill is called "not sick."
One who is able is one who is capable of wandering for alms.
One who is ill is one who is not capable of wandering for alms.
If one who is not ill accepts solid or soft food with the intention, "I will eat it," without having made an announcement, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession.

If, without an announcement being made, one perceives that no announcement has been made, and being not ill, one receives solid or soft food with one's own hand within the monastery and then eats or consumes it, there is an offense entailing confession.

If, when it has not been announced, one who is not ill, being in doubt, accepts hard food or soft food with his own hand within the monastery and then eats or consumes it, he commits an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).

If, when it has not been announced, one who is not ill, perceiving that it has been announced, accepts hard food or soft food with his own hand within the monastery and then eats or consumes it, he commits an offense entailing confession.
If he accepts for the purpose of food anything that is to be taken at the proper time, or for seven days, or for as long as life lasts, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For every mouthful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it has been announced, but one perceives it as not having been announced, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it has been announced, but one is uncertain about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it has been announced and he perceives that it has been announced, there is no offense. There is no offense if it has been announced.
If one eats the leftovers of a sick person after having informed them,
or if one receives food outside the monastery and eats it inside the monastery;
In that regard, one who eats the root, bark, leaf, flower, or fruit of a *jātaka* tree;
or who, when there is a reason, consumes what is to be used within a watch of the night, within seven days, or for life;
or one who is insane.
"For the first offender":
thus ends the fourth training rule on offenses entailing acknowledgment.
Venerable sirs, the four rules on offenses entailing acknowledgment have been recited.
In this matter, I ask the venerable ones:
"Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: [Are you pure in this?]
“Are you pure in this matter?
For a third time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter?”
"Venerable sirs, this matter is pure; therefore you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Section on the Offenses Entailing Confession is finished.
